texts.r:skill:e.e1.alpha: Words are easy to remember when you know their first sound and first letter. Say the sounds out loud as you read.
texts.r:skill:e.e1.greet: When you meet someone, say **Hello**. When you leave, say **Goodbye**. Say your name with **My name is ...**.
texts.r:skill:e.e1.numcol: Learn number words like one, two, three... and colour words like red, blue, yellow...
texts.r:skill:e.e1.family: mother (mum), father (dad), grandmother (grandma), baby (a very young child): these are words for people in your family.
texts.r:skill:e.e1.class: desk, chair, bag, pencil, book... Say the things in your classroom in English.
texts.r:skill:e.e2.noun: Words that name things, like rabbit (an animal with long ears), bird (an animal that flies) and fish (an animal that swims), are called **nouns**.
texts.r:skill:e.e2.verb: Words that show an action, like jump (go up in the air), run (move fast) and eat (have food), are called **verbs**.
texts.r:skill:e.e2.like: **I like ...** means you enjoy something. **I have ...** means something is yours.
texts.r:skill:e.e2.sent: After I, use **am**. After You, use **are**. A sentence goes in this order: 'who → what they are / what they do'.
texts.r:skill:e.e2.read: When you read, first look for the words from the question in the text.
texts.r:skill:e.e3.build: A sentence goes in this order: 'who → does → what'. After He, She or a person's name, add **-s** to the verb.
texts.r:skill:e.e3.pron: Instead of a name, you can use **He**, **She**, **It**, **They** or **We**.
texts.r:skill:e.e3.tense: For things happening now or again and again, use the **present**. For things that already happened, use the **past**: add **-ed** to the end of the verb.
texts.r:skill:e.e3.routine: get up, brush my teeth, eat breakfast, go to bed... Say your daily routine in English.
texts.r:skill:e.e3.read: Read the text and find who did what, and when.
texts.r:skill:e.e3.abc1: The alphabet has **capital letters** and **lowercase letters**. Many pairs look different, so learn them one pair at a time. Take special care with letters that look alike, such as b, d, p and q.
texts.r:skill:e.e3.snd1: The first sound of a word is linked to its first letter. Find words that begin with the same sound to learn how sounds and spelling are related. Sometimes two letters, such as ph, make the f sound.
texts.r:skill:e.e4.tense: For now or habits, use the **present**. For the past, add **-ed**. For things you will do, use **will + base verb**.
texts.r:skill:e.e4.qneg: Start a question with **Do/Does**. To say no, use **don't/doesn't**.
texts.r:skill:e.e4.adj: Words like big, small, hot and cold describe how something looks or feels.
texts.r:skill:e.e4.prep: Use **on**, **in**, **under** and **behind** to say where things are.
texts.r:skill:e.e4.read: Find who did what, and where, in the text, then answer.
texts.r:skill:e.e5.gram: Use **an** before a vowel sound and **a** before a consonant sound. For one thing, use **There is**. For many things, use **There are**.
texts.r:skill:e.e5.comp: To compare two things, use **-er + than**. For 'the most', use **the -est**. For long words, use **more**.
texts.r:skill:e.e5.future: For things you will do, use **will + base verb** or **be going to + base verb**.
texts.r:skill:e.e5.transform: For negatives, use **not / don't / doesn't / didn't**. For questions, put **Are / Do / Does** at the start of the sentence.
texts.r:skill:e.e5.read: Long texts are easier if you find who, where, when and what, as if you were underlining them.
texts.r:skill:e.e6.tense: For things happening now, use **be + -ing**. For the past, use the **past tense**. For the future, use **will / be going to**.
texts.r:skill:e.e6.modal: **can** (be able to), **must** (have to), **should** (it is a good idea to), **may** (it is OK to) are followed by the base form of the verb.
texts.r:skill:e.e6.vocab: Learn words with similar meanings and opposites together, and your vocabulary will double.
texts.r:skill:e.e6.read: Read a text with several sentences and find who did something, when and why.
texts.r:skill:e.e6.seq1: Words that show order, such as **First**, **Then / Next**, **After that** and **Finally**, tell you the order in which things happened.
texts.r:skill:e.e6.pun1: A sentence starts with a **capital letter** and ends with the right **punctuation mark**: a period (.) for a statement, a question mark (?) for a question, and an exclamation mark (!) for surprise or strong feeling. People's names and the word I are always capitalised.
texts.r:skill:e.vocab: Learn common words with **sound + meaning + spelling** together and you will remember them for a long time. Tap the speaker button to hear how they sound.
texts.r:skill:e.be: The verb be changes its form with the subject. **I → am**, **he / she / it → is**, **you / we / they → are**.
texts.r:skill:e.pres: When the subject is **he / she / it (third person singular)**, add **-s / -es** to the verb. Words ending in -ch, -sh, -s, -x, -o take -es. For consonant + y, change y to i and add -es!
texts.r:skill:e.plural: For two or more, usually add **-s** to the noun. Nouns ending in -x take **-es**. Learn irregular plurals by heart. A sentence goes **subject → verb → the rest**.
texts.r:skill:e.order: For two or more, usually add **-s** to the noun. Nouns ending in -x take **-es**. Learn irregular plurals by heart. A sentence goes **subject → verb → the rest**.
texts.r:skill:e.m2.perf: have/has + past participle. It shows experience, completion or continuation. Tell since (a point in time) apart from for (a length of time).
texts.r:skill:e.m2.pass: Use be + past participle to say that something is done to someone or something. Add the doer with by.
texts.r:skill:e.m2.inf: want, hope, decide + to-infinitive; enjoy, finish, avoid + gerund. stop + to V shows purpose, and stop + V-ing means stopping an action.
texts.r:skill:e.m2.comp: -er/-est and more/most. Use than with comparatives and the with superlatives. good → better → best is irregular.
texts.r:skill:e.m2.read: Read the question first, then find the clue sentence. The title and main idea cover the whole text.
texts.r:skill:e.m2.sum1: To summarise, find the **main idea** and shrink it to one or two sentences. A sentence about only one detail, one that adds something not in the passage, or one that is too broad is not a good summary.
texts.r:skill:e.m3.rel: Join two sentences into one with who (people), which (things), that (both) and whose (possession).
texts.r:skill:e.m3.cond: If + present, will + V (something possible). If + past, would + V (imagining something that is not true now).
texts.r:skill:e.m3.ques: Use the order question word + subject + verb. Do not use do/does/did.
texts.r:skill:e.m3.part: -ing is active or ongoing; -ed is passive or finished. For feelings, use -ing for what causes the feeling and -ed for the person who feels it.
texts.r:skill:e.m3.read: Put clues together to make an inference. Decide the purpose of a text by looking at its requests and claims.
texts.r:skill:e.h1.tense: had + p.p. is for something that happened before another past event. have been -ing is for an action that has continued until now.
texts.r:skill:e.h1.clause: where / when / why are relatives that work like adverbs. whether / that introduce noun clauses.
texts.r:skill:e.h1.partc: Drop the conjunction and the subject, and change the verb to -ing. The subject must be the same in both parts.
texts.r:skill:e.h1.conn: Tell apart cause and effect (so, therefore), contrast (however), examples (for example) and addition (in addition).
texts.r:skill:e.h1.main: The main idea is often after However, which turns a common belief around, and in the last sentence. Fill in a blank by following the flow problem → solution → result.
texts.r:skill:e.h2.inv: When Never/Hardly/Only then comes first, the order becomes auxiliary + subject. Use It is ~ that for emphasis.
texts.r:skill:e.h2.subj: In I wish / as if / If clauses, use the past for the opposite of the present and had p.p. for the opposite of the past.
texts.r:skill:e.h2.wh: whatever, whoever, whichever and however + adjective mean 'no matter what / who / which / how ...'.
texts.r:skill:e.h2.vocab: Guess the meaning of a new word from clues of contrast, example and cause, and from its prefix.
texts.r:skill:e.h2.logic: Follow the text using what pointing words refer to and the linking words. Gather the details to reach the conclusion.
texts.r:skill:e.h3.par: Phrases joined by and/but/or take the same form. The verb agrees with the main subject.
texts.r:skill:e.h3.tone: Find the mood from descriptive and emotional words. Find the purpose by checking if the text asks, informs or persuades.
texts.r:skill:e.h3.ins: Use linking words, pointing words and time order as clues to put sentences in order and find where a given sentence fits.
texts.r:skill:e.h3.col: Learn word pairs that go together, like make a decision, take a risk and heavy rain. Guess the meaning of idioms from the situation.
texts.r:skill:e.h3.sum: Find the key idea and the contrasting expressions in the text and shorten them into one sentence.
texts.r:skill:e.h.conv: In conversation questions, check not only that the grammar is correct but also that the tone sounds natural and polite in that situation. Offers, interrupting, responding to compliments, idioms and indirect speech come up often.
texts.r:skill:e.h.job: In workplace English, the key points are idioms (touch base), abbreviations (ASAP, etc.) and verb-preposition pairs (collocations). Don't translate word for word; remember them as chunks used in work situations.
texts.r:skill:e.h.media: In media English, it is important to tell facts from opinions and to judge whether the reasoning in a claim is sound. Remember terms such as image descriptions (alt text, caption) and editing tools by their purpose.
texts.r:skill:e.h.world: For world-culture topics, learn key words such as culture, diversity and stereotype, and expressions for trying to understand other cultures without judging them. Tell look-alike words apart using context clues.
texts.r:skill:e.h.lit: In literature questions, the key is to know the definition of a term and apply it to a scene in the story. Keep foreshadowing, symbol, point of view, theme and character roles distinct.
texts.r:skill:e.h.debate: Debate requires telling terms (motion, rebuttal, etc.), kinds of evidence and logical fallacies apart. When evaluating a claim, first ask, "What is the evidence for this?"
texts.r:skill:e.h.write: In writing, choose the form that fits the purpose and the reader, and check sentence components (subject and verb) and the logic of connectors. For specific texts like a resume, actions and numbers are better than vague words.
